title: Community
hookLine: a group to pray or talk with
tomorrow: who do you ask when you can't tell God's voice from your own?

cards: So who do you call when the faith gets lonely? Start with an odd detail in Matthew.

Jesus tells his listeners to pray by themselves, in the Douay-Rheims: "enter into thy chamber, and having shut the door, pray to thy Father in secret." A few lines later, he gives them the words to pray in that shut room.
Look for an I in them, or a my. There isn't one. Our Father.
Give us. Forgive us. Deliver us.

teach.h: OUR FATHER, BEHIND A SHUT DOOR.
teach.b: Here's the answer the prayer gives: in it, nobody is ever only one. Even alone, behind a shut door, the one praying says our, and stands inside a family.
Catholics put it this way: faith is personal, but never private. The first Christians lived it out in public.

Acts says they "were persevering in the doctrine of the apostles, and in the communication of the breaking of bread, and in prayers." Teaching, sharing, the bread, the prayers, and all of it together.
One word to tell a friend: persevering. These weren't people who came once for a big event.
They kept showing up. Then Jesus makes a promise about small groups, not stadiums: "where there are two or three gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them."
So a rule for life needs a few people, not a crowd: a parish Bible study, a young adult group, a few neighbors who pray the rosary, two friends who talk honestly about God over tacos.
People who'll notice when you stop coming, and ask.

how: Catholics find community in their parish and in smaller groups within it: Bible studies, prayer groups, young adult groups, rosary groups and campus ministries.

o: a social club that meets in the parish hall
a few people who pray and keep showing up together
a big crowd you see once a year at Christmas

games.q: the plural prayer — tap the pairs.
p: no I, no my: our, us
there am I in the midst of them

s: since Jesus said pray behind a shut door, faith is meant to be private
he sends you into the room with a prayer that says our: personal, never private.
Jesus promises to be present where two or three gather in his name
there am I in the midst of them. two or three is enough.
Acts says the first Christians came together once, for a big event
they were persevering: teaching, sharing, the bread and prayers, again and again.

games.q: you've joined a parish Bible study. after three weeks, one member is great, one talks too much, one never speaks. what does Acts suggest?
o: keep showing up. the first Christians persevered with each other, not with perfect people.
look for a better group whose people fit you right away.
stop going and pray the Our Father alone; it's the same prayer.
games.why: Acts calls them persevering. the point of two or three isn't a perfect fit; it's people who keep coming back.

practice: Pick up your phone and think of two people who might pray, read or just talk faith with you: a friend, a cousin, someone from the parish. Send one of them a short message asking if they'd want to meet once.
Then sit with the word our, and the faces it holds for you.

wordCard.voice: Community. Two or three gathered, persevering together, praying a prayer that says our even behind a closed door.

orig.note: Greek: sharing, fellowship. the word in Acts 2:42 the Douay-Rheims renders the communication.

carryVoice: Keep this one close: not alone, since even the shut-door prayer begins with our. Until tomorrow.
